name: Lauric acid

lead: Lauric acid is the main fatty acid in coconut oil and is used to make soaps and cleansing agents.
It is mentioned in acne talk because it inhibited some bacteria in laboratory tests; no skin trials were found.

paras: It acts as a surfactant in cleansers, and in lab studies disrupts bacterial membranes.
Pure lauric acid can irritate skin and eyes. Dietary intake raises total and LDL cholesterol in trials.

lead: Lauric acid (dodecanoic acid) is a saturated 12-carbon medium-chain fatty acid that makes up about half the fatty acids in coconut oil and palm kernel oil.[1][2] It is used mainly to make soaps and surfactants for cosmetics and cleansers.[1]

In skincare discussion it is cited for antimicrobial activity: a 1972 laboratory study of 30 fatty acids found lauric acid the most inhibitory saturated fatty acid against Gram-positive bacteria.[3] The wiki found no clinical trial of lauric acid applied to skin for acne or other appearance outcomes.

paras: Lauric acid is a white solid at room temperature that melts at roughly 43 to 48 C and dissolves poorly in water.[2] Coconut oil contains about 45 to 55 percent lauric acid and palm kernel oil a similar share; smaller amounts occur in human milk and laurel oil.[1][2] Theodor Marsson named it after laurel in 1842.[1]
Reacting lauric acid with alkali gives sodium laurate, a soap, and its derivatives act as emulsifying, cleansing and foaming agents in shampoos and cleansers.[1][2]

In vitro work found chain length strongly affects bactericidal activity of fatty acids, with lauric acid the most inhibitory saturated acid against Gram-positive organisms in that study.[3] Grokipedia says this has prompted interest in biomedical uses, and notes it can irritate skin and eyes on direct contact.[2] Laboratory activity has not been shown in the sources reviewed to translate into an acne treatment in people.

A meta-analysis of 60 controlled trials examined how individual dietary fatty acids change the ratio of total to HDL cholesterol; Wikipedia summarises that lauric acid raises total, LDL and HDL cholesterol.[1][4]
No studies found for lauric acid as a topical skin or appearance treatment. Registered human trials relate to diet and metabolism, for example NCT03481608 on dietary lauric acid.[5]

timeline.event: Theodor Marsson names lauric acid after separating it from laurel fat.[1]
